stem: A trough drug level is ordered for a medication that requires therapeutic drug monitoring. When should the nurse coordinate specimen collection?

options.A: At the medication-specific ordered time, typically when the drug level is lowest just before the next scheduled dose.
options.B: At any convenient time because dose timing does not affect trough interpretation.
options.C: Exactly one hour early for every medication because an early sample equals the true trough.
options.D: Without regard to dose timing because the laboratory automatically corrects mistimed specimens.

rationale: A trough level represents the lowest concentration in the dosing interval and is generally collected just before the next scheduled dose, according to medication-specific instructions. NCBI nursing pharmacology guidance emphasizes coordinating medication administration with the timing of peak and trough blood draws because the result is used for dose interpretation. A is correct.
educational_objective: Coordinate therapeutic drug monitoring specimens with medication-specific dosing times so trough results are interpretable.
source_organization: National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI Bookshelf)
source_version_date: Open RN nursing pharmacology text current as accessed 2026-08-17
source_claim_supported: A trough is drawn when the drug level is lowest, right before the next scheduled dose, and medication administration should be planned around timed blood draws.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential — monitor laboratory values and diagnostic/therapeutic test results
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — therapeutic drug monitoring

source_original.stem: A provider orders a trough drug level to be drawn at a specific time relative to the client's next medication dose, and a new nurse draws the sample an hour early since the unit happened to be quiet at that moment. The nurse understands that collecting this specimen at the wrong time, as just happened, can result in:

options.A: Draw a timed trough at the ordered time because mistiming can mislead dose interpretation
options.B: Draw a trough whenever convenient because timing has little effect on therapeutic monitoring
options.C: Draw every trough one hour early because early samples always equal the true minimum level
options.D: Ignore dose timing because laboratory calibration automatically corrects mistimed samples

source_original.rationale: For timed specimens such as trough drug levels, collecting the sample at the wrong time relative to the medication dose can result in an inaccurate result that does not truly reflect the intended measurement (such as the lowest point in the dosing interval), potentially leading to incorrect dosing decisions based on a misleading result — making precise timing critical for these specific tests.
source_original.source_detail: Therapeutic drug monitoring principles: peak/trough interpretation depends on specimen timing relative to dose; mistiming can mislead dosing decisions; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Re-sourced to a directly accessible NCBI nursing pharmacology chapter, removed the novice-error narrative, changed the blueprint from Safety and Infection Prevention and Control to Reduction of Risk Potential, and reduced difficulty to easy.

audit_findings.claim_audit: Trough timing relative to next dose is directly supported.

distractor_audit.D: False; lab cannot infer an unrecorded true trough.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: A includes the medication-specific qualifier and is unique.
audit_findings.blueprint: Lab/therapeutic monitoring is better mapped to Reduction of Risk Potential than Safety and Infection Prevention and Control.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked NCBI Peak and Trough Levels and blueprint mapping; A remains unique.
